real-estate-investment-calculator.quickAnswer: NOI = annual rent - operating expenses; cap rate = NOI / price; cash-on-cash = cash flow / cash invested; DSCR = NOI / debt service. Example: a 5,000,000 property renting at 50,000 per month with 10,000 monthly expenses has an NOI of 480,000 and a 9.6% cap rate. With 25% down plus 250,000 closing costs and an 8.5% 20-year loan, cash-on-cash is 5.97% and DSCR is 1.23, which lenders consider acceptable.
keyFacts: NOI (net operating income) is the property's profit before financing and income tax.
Cap rate values the property itself, independent of how you finance it.
GRM (gross rent multiplier) = price / annual rent; lower means cheaper relative to rent.
Cash-on-cash measures return on your actual cash invested, including closing costs.
DSCR (debt service coverage ratio) = NOI / annual loan payments; lenders usually want 1.2 or more.
Higher cap rates usually mean higher risk or weaker locations, not free money.
howTo: Enter the purchase price and total closing costs.
Enter the monthly rent and monthly operating expenses.
Enter your down payment percentage, loan rate, and term.
Read NOI, cap rate, and GRM for the property itself.
Read cash-on-cash and DSCR for your financed deal, and check the verdict.
real-estate-investment-calculator.formula:
NOI = (Rent - Expenses) x 12.
Cap rate = NOI / Price x 100.
GRM = Price / (Rent x 12).
Cash invested = Down payment + Closing costs.
Cash-on-cash = (NOI - Annual debt service) / Cash invested x 100.
DSCR = NOI / Annual debt service.
Example: 480,000 / 5,000,000 = 9.6% cap; 89,400 / 1,500,000 = 5.97% cash-on-cash.
benefits: The four metrics professionals use, computed together in seconds.
Cap rate compares properties regardless of financing structure.
DSCR verdict tells you instantly whether a lender would like the deal.
Including closing costs gives an honest cash-on-cash figure.
limitations: Uses one year's stabilized numbers; real income and expenses fluctuate.
Ignores appreciation, tax benefits, and principal paydown in total return.
Cap rate alone cannot value a property: location and condition dominate.
Not investment advice: verify rents, expenses, and title before investing.

faqs.q: What is a good cap rate?
faqs.a: It varies by market: 4 to 6% is common in prime metro areas, 7 to 10% in smaller cities and riskier assets. Compare cap rates only within the same market and property type. A very high cap rate usually signals high risk, not a bargain.

faqs.q: Cap rate vs cash-on-cash: which matters?
faqs.a: Both. Cap rate measures the property's own yield, ignoring your loan; cash-on-cash measures your personal return after financing. Use cap rate to compare properties, and cash-on-cash to compare financing choices on one property.
Most want 1.20 to 1.25 or higher, meaning NOI covers loan payments with a 20 to 25% cushion. Below 1.0 the property cannot service its own debt, and most lenders will decline the loan.
Lower is better: it means you pay fewer years of rent for the property. Residential GRMs of 8 to 12 are common in many markets. GRM is a rough screen only, since it ignores expenses entirely.

faqs.q: Should closing costs count in cash invested?
faqs.a: Yes. Stamp duty, registration, and brokerage are real cash out of your pocket that earns no return until the property performs. Including them, as this calculator does, gives the honest cash-on-cash figure.

faqs.q: Does a high cap rate mean a better investment?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Cap rates rise with risk: weak locations, old buildings, and unreliable tenants all push cap rates up. A high cap rate is the market's way of paying you to take that risk.

labels.dscrGood: DSCR of 1.2 or more: comfortably covers the loan payments.
labels.dscrThin: DSCR between 1.0 and 1.2: thin cushion, most lenders want more.
labels.dscrBad: DSCR below 1.0: rental income does not cover the loan payments.
